answer: Little's Law is an average identity, L = lambda x W, where W is the mean residence time of work inside one consistently defined boundary. It follows from long-run conservation of counts, so the latency input the identity requires is the arithmetic mean time in the system, not an arbitrary quantile of the latency distribution. A p99 is a threshold: it reports a value that at most 1% of requests exceed and says nothing by itself about the mean or the rest of the distribution. Substituting p99 for W changes the quantity being multiplied by throughput and normally overstates mean occupancy when the tail is heavy. The book's synthetic example makes the error concrete: 95% of requests at 0.10 s and 5% at 2.10 s give a mean of 0.20 s but a p99 of 2.10 s; at 120 completed operations/s, L = 120 x 0.20 = 24 average outstanding operations, whereas 120 x 2.10 = 252 would be an invalid use of the law and a misleading claim about required concurrency. The reverse also fails: a p99 does not determine the mean, because a single mean equation does not reveal the full latency distribution or guarantee an SLO. Correct practice is to measure mean residence time over a stable, consistently bounded window (admission to exit for any reason, with finite-window and rejection caveats handled) and to report p99 separately as a tail/SLO metric, not as W.
